newsitem.title: UK: Dollar testing lows against mark in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar testing lows against mark in late Europe.

text.p: The dollar was trading at session lows against the mark in late European trade, pushing below 1.50 marks on reports that Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said he saw no reason for the dollar to rise at the moment.
Although he said German exporters favoured a stronger dollar, dealers said his comments were giving the market an excuse to liquidate long dollar positions accumulated over the last week.
"There were a lot of longs around after the Bundesbank talked the dollar up last week, so these comments are providing a good excuse to get out," said a UK bank dealer.

The dollar lost almost half a pfennig against the mark after the comments and was trading at 1.5002/07 marks at 1644 GMT after dipping to a session low of 1.4990. It stood at 1.5084/89 marks late Friday in Europe.

By late trade, the dollar found support around the 1.50 mark level with dealers eyeing clarification of Welteke's comments from Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp, due to speak at 1730 GMT today.
Welteke's comments also saw the mark extend gains above 74 yen and firm slightly on an otherwise lacklustre European cross trade.
Market focus was now on German M3 money supply data due later this week and the IFO October business climate index due on Wednesday.

Some analysts expect the M3 data to be slightly distorted by the Deutsche Telekom flotation and see this week's figure as having less market influence than usual. Few expect any change in monetary policy at Thursday's Bundesbank council meeting.

U.S. trade data on Wednesday will also be watched in light of the 12.9 percent drop in Japan's October trade surplus. But dollar bulls were tempered by the first increase in the trade surplus with the U.S. in 20 months.

"The dollar may be a bit vulnerable in the near term against the yen ahead of the U.S. trade figures, but the decline in the Japanese surplus may give some support," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
An average of analysts' forecasts point to a September U.S. trade deficit of $9.5 billion compared with a $10.8 billion shortfall in August.
Sterling continued its climb higher, setting a fresh four-year high against the dollar on the back of surprise UK PSDR data. Sterling/mark also firmed but was off earlier highs.
